1.pericope_label: When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream

schools.summary: Augustine works from the older reading that has the returned as those who are comforted rather than as dreamers, asks how the captivity began and answers that men sold themselves by consenting to the seducer and could sell but not redeem themselves, and distinguishes a Zion eternal in angels from a Zion captive in men.

Calvin calls it unnatural and forced to read the psalm as prediction, has no doubt it was composed on the return itself, and translates the verb in the past tense; Gill takes the opposite view, allowing that the past tense may stand for the future and the psalm be a prophecy, renders the second verse as a future, and reports a Jewish commentary referring the whole to the world to come, besides assigning the third verse to the heathen rather than to the Jews.

Spurgeon reads the deliverance as so sudden that the freed felt like men out of themselves, quotes a couplet asking not to be woken if this be a dream, and applies the verse to conversion and to later emancipations from doubt and backsliding; Henry has the harps taken down from the willows and observes that they are never more tunable than after such a disuse, and holds that the captivity was meant not as dross put in the fire to be consumed but as gold to be refined.

Clarke notes the psalm has no title in the Hebrew or the versions, dates it to the close of the captivity, reports two guesses at its author, and tells at length how the Romans proclaimed liberty to the Greek cities by a herald at the games with the same effect as the decree of release had on the Jews; Wesley fixes simply on the surprise and astonishment.

Ellicott reports that the two oldest versions render the disputed word as consoled and that the Hebrew primarily means to be fat, being elsewhere rendered recover, a sense the Aramaic paraphrases adopt; he cites the same historian as Clarke on the same proclamation at the games, and his quotation supplies the psalm’s own figure of men wondering as at the empty show of a dream. Keil and Delitzsch hold the retrospect cannot be turned into the future without violating the syntax.

debates: Does the first verse look back or forward? Calvin calls it unnatural and forced to read it as prediction and translates the verb as a past; Keil and Delitzsch agree and hold that the reasons for a future reading are silenced by the requirements of the syntax, naming one translator as more consistent than others in attempting it; Gill takes the position they condemn, allowing the past tense to stand for the future and the psalm to be a prophecy, and reports a Jewish commentary referring it to the world to come.

What does the word rendered dream mean? Ellicott reports that the two oldest versions have as if consoled, and that the Hebrew primarily means to be fat and is elsewhere rendered recover, which the Aramaic paraphrases adopt; Augustine is found expounding the first of these alternatives, having it in his own text; the rest keep dreaming and take it of news too good to be believed.

Who speaks the third verse? Gill notes it is generally supposed the Jews are taking up what the heathen had said, but sees no reason why the heathen should not be speaking still, declaring the great things done to be for themselves also; Clarke keeps the words for the returned exiles and calls the last clause a burst of ecstatic joy.
outliers: Clarke and Ellicott independently reach for the same Roman historian’s account of a herald proclaiming liberty to the Greek cities at the games, and Ellicott’s quotation of it supplies the very simile of the psalm, that the hearers looked on one another like the empty show of a dream.

Henry has the harps taken down again from the willow-trees, and observes that they are never more melodiously tunable than after such a melancholy disuse, the long want of mercies greatly sweetening their return.
Augustine distinguishes a Zion eternal in angels from a Zion captive in men, and holds that a man was a citizen of that city but, sold under sin, became a pilgrim.
themes: a past tense read as a prophecy
deliverance too sudden to be believed
a pagan parallel supplying the psalm’s own figure
captivity described as refining rather than consuming
praise put into the mouths of the nations

4.pericope_label: Turn again our captivity, O Lord: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy

schools.summary: Henry has the returned still in distress in their own land while many remained abroad, so that they rejoiced with trembling, and draws the rule that the beginnings of mercy encourage us to pray for its completion, there being matter for prayer in this world even when we are best furnished with matter for praise.

Gill reports that some read the fourth verse as the prayer of the returned for those left behind, but prefers to carry it forward to the coming of the Redeemer or to a later conversion, gives two reasons why the sowing seed is called precious, and applies the sowing in tears to prayer and to the faithful preaching of the word.

Clarke suspects a great southward river behind the comparison of the fourth verse, allows the prayer to be either a recital of one used earlier or a petition for those still in the far provinces, notes that the captives returned at different times under different leaders, and expands the last verse into a scene of a poor farmer sowing his last saved seed in tears and returning in triumph with his sheaves; Wesley takes the comparison of floods sent into dry southern ground.

Ellicott renders the streams as channels and refers them to the sudden filling of dry torrent-beds in the southern district during the rains, reporting that the Greek version read a south wind and imagined a thaw instead; he prefers singing to joy in the fifth verse, contrasts harvest-home songs with the anxiety of seed-time, and holds that the poet found the closing proverb already current and touched it with a consecrating hand. Keil and Delitzsch likewise have the land thirsting as the southern country toward the desert thirsts.

debates: What is compared to the streams in the south? Clarke suspects a great river rising far south and running northward through several countries, while allowing that other rapid southward rivers might be meant; Ellicott renders the word channels and refers it to the sudden filling of dry torrent-beds in the southern district during the rainy season, so that the prayer asks for torrents of returning people to pour into a deserted land; Wesley, Henry and Keil and Delitzsch all take it the same way, of floods sent into parched southern ground. Ellicott adds that the Greek version read a south wind and evidently imagined the melting of a frozen stream.

For whom is the fourth verse prayed? Gill reports the reading that makes it the prayer of those already home for the brethren left behind, but prefers to refer it to the coming of the Redeemer or to a conversion still future; Henry keeps it historical and doubles it, since the returned were still in distress and many remained abroad; Clarke allows it may be a recital of a prayer used before the deliverance; Ellicott takes it simply of the many still dispersed among the nations.
outliers: Ellicott holds that the closing proverb was probably already current when the poet found it, and that he touched it with the consecrating hand until it became only less precious than a saying of divine lips about mourners being comforted.

Clarke expands the last verse into a scene of a poor farmer who has saved a little seed out of a famine, commits it to the furrow with a sorrowful heart and waters it in effect with his tears, and after a mild season fills his arms and carriages with sheaves and returns in triumph to his expecting family.
Gill gives two reasons why the seed is called precious, either that it was bought at a great price when grain was dear, or that the choicest wheat is what men keep for sowing.
themes: a deliverance begun and prayed forward to completion
dry watercourses filled in a single season
a common saying taken up and consecrated
tears counted as the watering of the seed
a harvest promised to those who must sow first
